title: Hydroxychloroquine as adjunctive therapy in steroid-dependent pediatric Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease with liver dysfunction: A case report.
abstract: Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease is usually self-limiting, but treatment of steroid-dependent disease in children remains uncertain. We report a 7-year-old girl with biopsy-confirmed Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease and severe liver dysfunction. She presented with intermittent fever and cervical lymphadenopathy, followed by rash and worsening liver dysfunction. Cervical lymph node biopsy revealed necrotizing lymphadenitis without evidence of malignancy. Antinuclear and U1 ribonucleoprotein antibodies were positive; liver-kidney microsomal type 1 antibodies were subsequently detected. Serologic tests for the viruses examined were negative, although hepatitis A testing was not performed. Retrospective assessment using the revised International Autoimmune Hepatitis Group scoring system did not reach the threshold for probable autoimmune hepatitis. Nevertheless, autoimmune hepatitis could not be excluded because liver histology was unavailable and the viral evaluation was incomplete. After relapse during prednisolone tapering, she received methylprednisolone pulse therapy followed by prednisolone and hydroxychloroquine. Remission was achieved, allowing gradual corticosteroid tapering. Prednisolone was discontinued at month 39 and hydroxychloroquine at month 50 after disease onset. No relapse occurred during the subsequent 8-month follow-up. No hydroxychloroquine-related adverse events, including retinopathy, were observed during 44 months of treatment or the subsequent follow-up. This case adds to the limited experience with prolonged hydroxychloroquine use in younger children with steroid-dependent Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease. Hydroxychloroquine may have contributed to corticosteroid tapering, although its independent efficacy cannot be established because it was initiated alongside intensified corticosteroid therapy.

title: Primary Sjögren's Syndrome Presenting With Complete Atrioventricular Block and Myocardial Injury: A Rare Immune-Mediated Cardiac Case Report.
abstract: Primary Sjögren's syndrome (pSS) is a systemic autoimmune disorder predominantly involving exocrine glands; cardiac complications represent rare extra-glandular manifestations, and complete atrioventricular block (CAVB) is uncommon. We report a 58-year-old female presenting with acute chest tightness and transient loss of consciousness. Her electrocardiogram showed CAVB with ventricular escape rhythm and elevated cardiac troponin-I. Emergency coronary angiography excluded significant obstructive coronary artery disease. Positive anti-SSA, anti-SSB, anti-Ro52, cardiac-specific autoantibodies, together with minor salivary gland biopsy, confirmed pSS. She received methylprednisolone and hydroxychloroquine for immunomodulation, plus dual-chamber permanent pacemaker implantation for persistent symptomatic conduction defects. Symptoms resolved and cardiac biomarkers normalized in short-term follow-up. This case alerts clinicians to pSS-related immune-mediated cardiac injury as a differential diagnosis for unexplained CAVB after excluding coronary artery disease.
